# I. Authors

Nguyen Ha --- M.S. in Computer Science.\
Yanglin Hu --- M.S. in Data Science.

# II. Problem Description

Clothing material drives comfort, durability, and satisfaction, yet Amazon listings usually bury it in free-text bullets rather than a searchable field. We ask two questions: can a model infer a product's dominant material from its listing text, and does material, with price and department, help predict the product's average rating?

# III. Data Summary

We use the Clothing, Shoes and Jewelry category of Amazon Reviews 2023 (Hou et al.): metadata for about 7.2 million products, each with a title, feature bullets, description, price, department, and average rating. We label each product by parsing composition strings such as "90% Polyester, 10% Spandex," taking the highest-percentage fiber and grouping rare materials into about ten classes.

# IV. Methods

For material, we compare TF-IDF with logistic regression or a linear SVM against fine-tuned DistilBERT (Sanh et al.), with composition strings removed from the input so the task is not a lookup. For ratings, we compare random forest and XGBoost (Chen and Guestrin) regressors with a mean-rating baseline. We use five-fold cross-validation and report macro-F1 (classes are imbalanced) and RMSE/MAE. Challenges are noisy shoe labels, missing prices, and scale (we use a fixed-seed sample).

# V. Preliminary Results

On the first 10,000 metadata records, only 3.6% of products store material in a structured field, but 46.0% give a percentage composition in their bullets and 79.0% name a known material. The top materials are polyester (24.3%), cotton (22.0%), leather (14.3%), and rubber (13.5%, mostly shoe soles). Price is missing for 45.7% of products.
